questions.stem: A 35-year-old male patient with a history of epilepsy presents to your clinic. He has been taking phenytoin for several years to control his seizures. Which of the following is not an adverse effect of phenytoin?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Hypertension

 

Option C:

 

  • Phenytoin is an antiepileptic medication that is commonly used to treat seizures.
  • It can cause several adverse effects, including:
    • Hypertrophy of gums: Phenytoin can cause overgrowth of the gum tissue, leading to a condition known as gingival hyperplasia.
    • Hirsutism: Phenytoin can cause excessive hair growth, particularly in women.
    • Hypersensitivity: Phenytoin can cause an allergic reaction in some patients, leading to symptoms such as rash, fever, and swollen lymph nodes.
  • However, hypertension is not a common adverse effect of phenytoin. It can cause cardiovascular effects such as hypotension and arrhythmias, but not hypertension.

bri,sans-serif">Explanation:

 

Option A. Decreases GABA uptake at the synaptic cleft: Incorrect, vigabatrin does not decrease GABA uptake; it increases GABA availability by inhibiting its breakdown.

Additionally, it is the drug of choice for infantile spasms related to tuberous sclerosis, but potential side effects include irreversible visual field defects and behavioral changes.

questions.stem: All the following drugs are NMDA receptor blockers except.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Diltiazem

 

Option D:

 

N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors are ionotropic glutamate receptors found in the central nervous system (CNS). These receptors are involved in synaptic plasticity, which is the process by which neurons adapt and change their strength in response to stimuli, including learning and memory. The activation of NMDA receptors requires both glutamate and glycine or D-serine, as well as the removal of a magnesium ion that blocks the channel at resting membrane potentials. The influx of calcium ions through the open channel leads to the activation of various intracellular signalling pathways, which can have both beneficial and detrimental effects on neuronal function.

 

NMDA receptor blockers are drugs that inhibit the activity of NMDA receptors. They can be classified as either competitive or non-competitive antagonists, depending on the mechanism of action. Competitive antagonists bind to the same site as the agonist, whereas non-competitive antagonists bind to a separate site on the receptor. Clinically useful drugs are all non-competitive NMDA antagonists.

M:        Methadone, Memantine, Magnesium

D:         Dextromethorphan

A:         Acamprosate, Amantadine

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female patient with a history of epilepsy presents to the emergency room with a prolonged seizure. According to her relatives, she has been experiencing convulsions for over 10 minutes. Which of the following is the drug of choice for the treatment of status epilepticus in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lorazepam

 

Option B:

 

Status epilepticus is a medical emergency that requires prompt treatment to prevent neurological damage and other complications. The first-line treatment for status epilepticus is usually a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam, which can help to rapidly terminate the seizure activity. Lorazepam has a longer duration of action compared to diazepam and is less likely to cause respiratory depression.

 

If the seizure continues despite benzodiazepine treatment, the next step is typically to administer a second-line antiepileptic medication, such as phenytoin or Fosphenytoin.

questions.stem: A boy aged 14 years was brought to the hospital emergency with crush injury of both lower legs. An eyewitness who brought the boy said that a bus had run over his legs about 20 min. ago. The legs were crushed but he had not bled much. He also said that initially the boy was shrieking in pain but had fainted on the way to the hospital. Preliminary examination reveals that the patient is in a semiconscious state, looks pale, the pulse is fast, low volume and collapsing. Both legs have sustained multiple fractures, the skin and soft tissues have lacerated from which blood is oozing, but there is no active bleeding. There is no apparent head injury. Which drug should be administered immediately, before even completing a thorough physical examination?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Morphine

 

Option C:

 

In this case, the boy has suffered a traumatic crush injury to both lower legs with multiple fractures and lacerations. He is in a semiconscious state, pale, with a fast and weak pulse, indicating that he may be in shock. Symptoms and signs indicate that the patient is going into neurogenic shock due to the excruciating pain of the crush injury. As such, the priority is to relieve acute pain.

 

Morphine is an appropriate choice for managing the patient's pain and can also help to reduce anxiety. It has vasodilatory effects which can help to stabilize the patient's blood pressure. However, the use of morphine should be carefully monitored due to the risk of respiratory depression, especially in a patient with hemodynamic instability.

Option B. Dobutamine is a positive inotropic agent that can increase cardiac output, but it is not the first-line treatment in this situation.

Option D. Levodopa is a first-line drug in the treatment of hepatic coma: Incorrect, as levodopa is not used for hepatic coma, which is related to liver failure and not typically managed with dopamine precursors.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Only a small fraction (about 1-3%) of administered levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier to become active in the brain, necessitating the co-administration of carbidopa to inhibit its peripheral metabolism and increase its central availability and effectiveness in treating Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: A patient is operated on for bile duct stricture. Post operatively he is receiving 3 ml epidural morphine for pain relief. One day he accidentally received 12 ml of morphine. What will not occur?
questions.solutionHtml:
>Ans. A) Tachycardia

 

Explanation:

 

  • Epidural administration of morphine can provide excellent pain relief, but it can also lead to adverse effects such as respiratory depression, urinary retention, and pruritus (severe itching). The risk of adverse effects is higher if the patient receives an overdose of morphine.
  • Tachycardia is not a common adverse effect of morphine, and it is not expected to occur in response to an overdose. Rather bradycardia can be seen due to depression of cardiovascular centre in brain.
  • Vomiting and retching are common adverse effects of morphine and can occur with an overdose.
  • Respiratory depression is the most significant adverse effect of morphine and can be life-threatening in severe cases.
  • Urinary retention is another common adverse effect of morphine that occurs due to the inhibition of bladder contractions.
  • Severe itching, or pruritus, is another common adverse effect of morphine that can be bothersome for the patient.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman with a history of bipolar disorder has been taking lithium throughout her pregnancy. Her neonate should be screened for which of the following?

The educational goal is to recognize the teratogenic risks associated with the use of lithium during pregnancy, particularly the increased risk of cardiac anomalies such as Ebstein's anomaly in the neonate.

questions.stem: False statement regarding phenytoin is?

options.text: It is a microsomal enzyme inducer.

options.label: D
options.text: It follows zero order kinetics at lower doses.

questions.answerText: It follows zero order kinetics at lower doses.
questions.solutionHtml:
y">Explanation:

 

Option A. It is highly protein bound: This is true. Phenytoin is approximately 90% bound to plasma proteins, and because of this, it can be displaced by other drugs, leading to an increase in the concentration of free (active) phenytoin.
 

Option B. Its half-life increases with increase in dose: This is true and is related to phenytoin's zero order kinetics at therapeutic or higher doses. As the dose increases, the half-life becomes longer because the drug-metabolizing enzymes in the liver become saturated.

Educational Objective:

 

The educational goal is to understand the pharmacokinetics of phenytoin, an antiepileptic drug. At lower doses, phenytoin follows first order kinetics, but as the dose increases and reaches therapeutic levels, it exhibits zero order kinetics where the drug is metabolized at a constant rate.

questions.stem: The risk of carbamazepine induced Stevens Johnson syndrome is increased in the presence of which of the following gene?
questions.solutionHtml:
ri,sans-serif">Ans. B) HLA-B 1502

 

Explanation:

 

Carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) are serious skin reactions that can be life-threatening. These conditions are significantly more likely to occur in individuals who have the HLA-B 1502 gene variant. This genetic marker is notably prevalent in populations of Asian descent, leading to heightened risk assessments and screening recommendations before the administration of carbamazepine in these populations. Testing for the presence of HLA-B 1502 is recommended to prevent the initiation of carbamazepine in patients at increased risk of developing SJS/TEN, thereby enhancing patient safety.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Screening for the HLA-B 1502 gene variant in patients who are candidates for carbamazepine therapy, particularly those of Asian ancestry, is crucial in reducing the risk of potentially fatal skin reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. This preemptive approach is a vital component of personalized medicine, aimed at ensuring the safety and efficacy of drug treatments.

Benzodiazepines enhance but do not mimic the action of GABA, functioning as allosteric modulators rather than direct agonists of GABA A receptors, which is crucial for understanding their safety profile and therapeutic effects.

questions.stem: A bank employee suffering from depression came to AIIMS OPD. He was started on Escitalopram. Which of the following adverse effects cannot be explained with Escitalopram?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Bradycardia

 

Option C:

 

Escitalopram, a commonly used selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), has various known side effects that impact both the central nervous system and other bodily functions, but bradycardia is not typically one of them. Instead, SSRIs like Escitalopram are more likely to cause side effects such as:

 

Option A. Vivid dreaming: This can be a result of increased serotonin levels affecting various neurotransmitter pathways, including those that influence sleep and dreaming.

 

Option B. Anorgasmia: Sexual dysfunction is a well-documented side effect of SSRIs, which can interfere with sexual arousal and orgasm, likely through their effects on serotonin receptors that impact sexual function.

 

Option D. Nausea: This is a common initial side effect when starting SSRIs, resulting from the increased serotonin activity in the gastrointestinal tract.

 

Bradycardia, or a slower than normal heart rate, is not a typical reaction to Escitalopram. SSRIs can cause some cardiovascular effects, but they are more commonly associated with mild tachycardia rather than bradycardia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

While Escitalopram is effective for treating depression and associated symptoms like anxiety, its adverse effects can impact sexual function, sleep, and gastrointestinal health but not typically heart rate in the form of bradycardia

questions.stem: All the following pairs of mechanism of action with the drug are correct except
questions.solutionHtml:
e:12.0pt">Ans. B) Selective MAO- B inhibitor– Clorgyline

 

Explanation:

 

  • Clorgyline is a non-selective monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitor means it inhibits both MAO-A as well as MAO-B isoforms. MAO-A and MAO-B are enzymes involved in the breakdown of neurotransmitters such as dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin. MAO inhibitors can be used to treat depression and Parkinson's disease, as they can increase the levels of these neurotransmitters in the brain.
  • Benserazide is a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor that is used in combination with levodopa to treat Parkinson's disease. It works by inhibiting the enzyme dopa decarboxylase, which converts levodopa into dopamine outside the brain. This allows more levodopa to cross the blood-brain barrier and increase dopamine levels in the brain.
  • Entacapone is a Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) inhibitor that is used in combination with levodopa to treat Parkinson's disease. It works by inhibiting the enzyme COMT, which breaks down levodopa in the peripheral tissues. This allows more levodopa to cross the blood-brain barrier and increase dopamine levels in the brain.
  • Amantadine is an antiviral medication that is also used to treat Parkinson's disease. It works by increasing the release of dopamine in the brain and blocking the reuptake of dopamine into the presynaptic neuron.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding smoking addiction?

options.label: A
options.text: Nicotine gums have 10-15% more bioavailability than nicotine lozenges.

options.label: B

questions.answerText: Varenicline is ideal but has a risk of cardiovascular events.

Ans. B) Varenicline is ideal but has a risk of cardiovascular events.

 

Option B:

 

  • Varenicline is a medication used to aid in smoking cessation. It works by blocking the effects of nicotine in the brain, reducing cravings and withdrawal symptoms. Studies have shown that varenicline is more effective than nicotine replacement therapy or bupropion for smoking cessation.
  • However, there is a risk of cardiovascular events associated with varenicline use, particularly in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Patients should be monitored closely for cardiovascular events while taking varenicline.

Option C. Efficiency of nicotine gums increases after coffee or tea intake:  Caffeine can decrease the effectiveness of nicotine replacement therapy. Therefore, a gap of 15 minutes must be observed between use of NRT and drinking tea or coffee.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old patient with a history of Parkinson's disease presents to the clinic complaining of peripheral numbness and tingling in his fingers and toes. n>

 

Option A. Ropinirole: While also a dopamine agonist, it does not commonly cause peripheral vasospasm.

 

Option B. Levodopa: The most commonly used medication in Parkinson's treatment, known for many side effects, but peripheral vasospasm is not typically one of them.

 

Option D. Entacapone: A COMT inhibitor used to extend the effects of Levodopa; not associated with causing peripheral vasospasm.

Bromocriptine can cause peripheral vasospasm leading to symptoms like numbness and tingling in extremities, an important consideration when monitoring side effects in Parkinson’s disease patients.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male patient with a history of opioid addiction presents to your clinic for treatment. He has a long history of opioid use and has recently stopped using opioids. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of methadone, the medication that is commonly used to treat opioid addiction?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Opioid receptor agonist.

 

Option A:

 

  • Methadone is a synthetic opioid that is primarily used to treat opioid addiction by reducing withdrawal symptoms and cravings. It works by binding to the same opioid receptors in the brain that are targeted by natural opioids, such as endorphins, to produce pain relief, euphoria, and other effects.
  • Opioid receptor partial agonists, such as buprenorphine, have a weaker effect on the opioid receptors than full agonists like methadone.
  • Opioid receptor antagonists, such as naloxone and naltrexone, block the effects of opioids and are used to treat opioid overdose and prevent relapse in individuals who have stopped using opioids.

questions.stem: Chlorpromazine acts on which of the following receptors? D2 and 5HT2 receptors GABA and Beta-adrenergic receptors Muscarinic M1 and alpha-adrenergic receptors H1 receptors
questions.solutionHtml:
e:12.0pt">Ans. A) 1, 3 and 4 are correct.

 

Explanation:

 

Chlorpromazine, a first-generation antipsychotic, has a broad receptor profile that contributes to both its therapeutic effects and side effects:

 

  • D2 and 5HT2 receptors: It acts as an antagonist at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5HT2 receptors, which helps modulate mood and psychotic symptoms.
  • Muscarinic M1 and alpha-adrenergic receptors: It also antagonizes these receptors, contributing to side effects such as dry mouth, sedation, and hypotension.
  • H1 receptors: Histamine receptor antagonism leads to sedative effects, which is typical of many first-generation antipsychotics.

 

GABA and Beta-adrenergic receptors: Chlorpromazine does not significantly interact with these receptor types, making statement 2 incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chlorpromazine's action on multiple neurotransmitter receptors explains both its efficacy in treating psychotic symptoms and its wide range of potential side effects, underscoring the importance of careful patient monitoring when using this medication.



ul patient monitoring when using this medication.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old male with schizophrenia was treated with haloperidol 5 mg once daily at bedtime, which was increased to 7.5 mg daily in the 2nd week and 10 mg daily in the 3rd week. His symptoms improved, but in the 5th week, his family reported that his restlessness had returned, and he kept pacing around in the room, though he was not aggressive. questions.solutionHtml:

The patient's symptoms suggest that he may be experiencing akathisia, a side effect of antipsychotic medications like haloperidol. Akathisia is characterized by restlessness, an uncontrollable urge to move, and difficulty in sitting still.

 

Propranolol, a beta-blocker, is often used to treat akathisia and could be an appropriate choice to address the patient's symptoms.

Option C. Valbenazine is used to treat tardive dyskinesia, a different movement disorder associated with long-term antipsychotic use. It is not indicated for treating akathisia.

 

Option D. Dantrolene is a muscle relaxant used to treat muscle spasms and malignant hyperthermia. It is not used to treat akathisia.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presented to a hospital with focal seizures. His renal function was normal. Which of the following is the drug of choice for this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
amily:Calibri,sans-serif">Ans. D) Carbamazepine

 

Explanation:

 

  • Carbamazepine (DOC) and oxcarbazepine (related drug), phenytoin, lamotrigine and levetiracetam are currently the first line drugs approved for the initial treatment of focal seizures, including those that secondarily generalize. Overall, they have very similar efficacy, but differences in pharmacokinetics and toxicity are the main determinants for use in each patient.
  • An advantage of carbamazepine is that its metabolism follows first-order pharmacokinetics, and the relationship between drug dose, serum levels, and toxicity is linear.
  • Oxcarbazepine has the advantage of lesser enzyme induction (and thus drug interactions) than carbamazepine. However, it has more association with dilutional hyponatremia than carbamazepine.
  • Lamotrigine tends to be well-tolerated in terms of side effects. However, patients need to be particularly vigilant about the possibility of a skin rash during the initiation of therapy. This can be extremely severe and lead to Stevens-Johnson syndrome if unrecognized and if the medication is not discontinued immediately.
  • Valproic acid is an effective alternative for some patients with partial seizures, especially when the seizures secondarily generalize.

The educational objective is to recognize ACTH as a first-line treatment option for infantile spasms.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient presents to your clinic with symptoms of depression. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of nortriptyline, a medication that can be used to treat his depression?

Nortriptyline is a TCA that acts predominatly as NA reuptake inhibitor unlike other TCAs which inhibit reuptake of both serotonin and nor-adrenaline.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old male patient with a history of alcohol use disorder presents to your clinic for treatment. He has a long history of heavy drinking and has recently stopped drinking. questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Naltrexone.

 

Option B:

 

  • Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist medication that is used to treat alcohol use disorder by reducing the craving for alcohol and preventing relapse in individuals who have stopped drinking.   • Methadone is an opioid agonist medication that is primarily used to treat opioid addiction by reducing withdrawal symptoms and cravings.
  • Naloxone and nalmefene are also opioid antagonist medications, but they are primarily used to reverse opioid overdose and are not typically used in the treatment of alcohol use disorder.

questions.stem: Which drug has inverse agonist activity at benzodiazepine receptors?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Beta carboline

 

Option B:

 

Beta-carbolines are compounds that have been identified to possess inverse agonist activity at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor. Unlike benzodiazepines, which are agonists at this site and increase the inhibitory effect of GABA leading to sedation and anxiolysis, inverse agonists like beta-carbolines decrease the action of GABA. This can lead to effects opposite those of benzodiazepines, such as increased anxiety and seizures in susceptible individuals.

 

Explanatio:

 

Option A. Flumazenil: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist, not an inverse agonist. It is used to reverse the effects of benzodiazepines in cases of overdose.

 

Option C. Naltrexone: Naltrexone is an opioid receptor antagonist used primarily in the management of alcohol and opioid dependence, not related to benzodiazepine receptor

 

Option D. Zopiclone: Zopiclone is a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic agent used for the treatment of insomnia. It acts as an agonist at the benzodiazepine site of the GABA-A receptor, similar to benzodiazepines, but it is not an inverse agonist.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The educational goal is to understand the concept of inverse agonism at the benzodiazepine receptors, exemplified by compounds such as beta-carbolines. This understanding highlights the diversity of drug actions at the GABA-A receptor complex, ranging from agonists (e.g., benzodiazepines) that enhance GABAergic activity to inverse agonists that reduce this activity, with significant implications for their effects on the central nervous system.

Ans. D) Liraglutide

 

Option D:

 

Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist that is approved for the treatment of obesity. It works by mimicking the action of the GLP-1 hormone, which is involved in appetite regulation and calorie intake. Liraglutide promotes weight loss by increasing feelings of fullness, reducing hunger, and thereby lowering calorie intake. It is administered via injection and is used as part of a comprehensive weight management program that includes diet, exercise, and behavior modification.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Sibutramine: Sibutramine was previously used for the treatment of obesity. However, it was withdrawn from the market in many countries due to concerns over cardiovascular side effects, including increased risk of heart attack and stroke. Therefore, it is no longer recommended or available as a treatment option for obesity.

 

Option B. Fenfluramine: Fenfluramine, part of the fen-phen combination, was used in the past for weight loss. However, it was withdrawn from the market due to its association with serious heart valve problems and pulmonary hypertension. It is no longer available or recommended for the treatment of obesity.

 

Option C.  Metformin: Metformin is primarily used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. While it is not approved specifically for the treatment of obesity, it may lead to modest weight loss in some individuals, especially those with insulin resistance. questions.stem: A female patient who has been on lithium therapy for bipolar disorder for 6 months presents with seizures, coarse tremors, confusion, and weakness of limbs after fasting for a few days due to religious reasons. To diagnose her condition, the following test should be performed:
questions.solutionHtml:
tr" lang="EN-US" style="font-size:12.0pt">Ans. B) Serum lithium levels

 

Explanation:

 

  • The patient's symptoms are suggestive of lithium toxicity, which can be confirmed by measuring serum lithium levels. Fasting and dehydration may have contributed to the development of lithium toxicity, as they can cause reduced renal clearance and increased reabsorption of lithium, leading to higher serum concentrations.

Other Options:

 Option C. ECG:  An ECG  may be necessary to check for any cardiac abnormalities, as lithium can sometimes affect the heart.

Option D. MRI: An MRI (D) may be considered if there is concern for other underlying neurological issues, but it is not the first step in diagnosing lithium toxicity.

questions.stem: A patient with bipolar disorder was treated with lithium. Hydrochlorothiazide was prescribed for his hypertension. He developed nausea, vomiting, coarse tremors and brisk reflexes 2 weeks after taking drugs. What is the likely reason for this presentation?

options.label: C
options.text: Increased renal tubular reabsorption of lithium.

options.label: D
options.text: Thiazide acts as an add on drug to lithium.

questions.answerText: Increased renal tubular reabsorption of lithium.
questions.solutionHtml:
Other Options:

 

Option A. Side effects of hydrochlorothiazide: While hydrochlorothiazide can cause side effects like electrolyte imbalances and dehydration, its common side effects do not typically include the combination of symptoms seen in lithium toxicity (nausea, vomiting, coarse tremors, and brisk reflexes). These symptoms are more specifically indicative of lithium toxicity rather than direct side effects of hydrochlorothiazide.
 

Option B. Decreased metabolism of hydrochlorothiazide by lithium: Lithium does not significantly impact the metabolism of hydrochlorothiazide. The metabolism and clearance of hydrochlorothiazide are primarily renal and are not substantially altered by concurrent lithium use, making this option an unlikely cause of the patient's symptoms.
 

Option D. Thiazide acts as an add-on drug to lithium: There is no evidence to suggest that thiazide diuretics act as add-on drugs to enhance the therapeutic effects of lithium in the treatment of bipolar disorder. The interaction between hydrochlorothiazide and lithium that is of clinical significance relates to the effect on lithium's renal handling, rather than a synergistic effect on mood stabilization.
 

Educational Objective:

 

The key learning point from this scenario is understanding the pharmacological interaction between lithium and thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide, and how this interaction can lead to increased serum lithium levels and subsequent lithium toxicity.

questions.answerText: Blood level below 350 ng/ml should be maintained to avoid agranulocytosis.
questions.solutionHtml:
span>

 

Explanation:

 

The false statement about clozapine is option B, which states that "Blood level below 350 ng/ml should be maintained to avoid agranulocytosis." This statement is not true because there is no specific blood level of clozapine that is associated with the risk of agranulocytosis, which is dose-independent adverse effect of clozapine. High plasma concentration of Clozapine increases the risk of seizures (dose-dependent). However, the usual plasma concentration required in many people is 300-600 ng/ml.

  • Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic drug that has high potency to block 5HT2 receptors as compared to D2 receptors. However, it also blocks D4 receptors, muscarinic receptors, alpha receptors and H1 receptors.
  • It suppresses both positive as well as negative symptoms of schizophrenia. It is the first FDA approved drug for anti-suicide indication.
  • It is used only as a reserve drug due to the risk of precipitation of seizures (even in non-epileptics) and agranulocytosis. Convulsions are dose-dependent adverse effects seen only at higher doses whereas agranulocytosis is independent of dose.
  • Clozapine should be started at low doses (12.5 mg) and gradually dose should be increased. Baseline WBC counts should be measured, and then weekly counts should be done at least for the first 6 months. When WBC count becomes less than 3000/mm3 or absolute neutrophil count becomes less than 1500/mm3, Clozapine should be discontinued. After discontinuation, weekly WBC counts should be measured for an additional 4 weeks.
  • It should not be used with Carbamazepine due to two reasons:
    • Carbamazepine induces its metabolism and thus decreases plasma concentration.
    • Carbamazepine has bone marrow suppressant action and can add to agranulocytosis caused by Clozapine.

Explanation:

 

The mainstay of treatment for Parkinson's disease is the use of dopaminergic medications, which increase the levels of dopamine in the brain. These medications can be

 

  1. Dopamine precursors: These medications are converted into dopamine in the brain and include levodopa (L-dopa) and its combination with carbidopa. Carbidopa prevents the breakdown of levodopa in the bloodstream (by inhibiting dopa decarboxylase enzyme), allowing more of it to reach the brain.

Explanation:

 

Fosphenytoin offers several advantages over phenytoin, particularly in how it is administered:

 

  • It is a water-soluble prodrug of phenytoin, meaning it is converted into phenytoin once administered. This conversion allows it to be more versatile and manageable in clinical settings.
  • Less damaging to the vein intima: Fosphenytoin is less irritating to the veins compared to phenytoin, which is known for causing phlebitis and damage to the vein walls.

Educational Objective:

 

Fosphenytoin provides critical advantages for intravenous use over phenytoin, particularly its solubility, less vein irritation, and flexibility in dilution options, making it preferable in emergency and hospital settings for rapid seizure control.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male patient complained of hearing voices and was started on haloperidol for the treatment of his symptoms. However, for the past few days, he has been very restless and constantly moving about. What is the most likely condition that the patient is experiencing?
questions.solutionHtml:
size:11pt">Explanation:

 

Option B. Tardive dyskinesia: This condition involves involuntary, repetitive movements of the face and limbs but typically develops after long-term use of antipsychotics, making it less likely in this acute setting.

 

Option C. Rabbit syndrome: Characterized by rapid movements of the lips and mouth, rabbit syndrome is associated with prolonged antipsychotic use, not acute symptoms following recent medication initiation.

 

Option D. Acute dystonia: While this involves sudden muscle contractions, it usually presents as twisted postures or abnormal movements of the face, neck, and eyes, rather than the restlessness and constant movement typical of akathisia.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Akathisia is a significant side effect of antipsychotic medications like haloperidol, presenting as an uncontrollable urge to move and restlessness, often occurring shortly after the initiation or increase of medication. Monitoring and managing this side effect are crucial for patient comfort and treatment adherence. Propranolol is frequently used to treat this condition effectively.

questions.stem: Treatment of choice for delirium tremens in alcohol withdrawal in a patient with severe alcoholic liver disease is?
questions.solutionHtml:
alibri,sans-serif">Ans. C) Lorazepam

 

Explanation:

 

  • Delirium tremens is a severe form of alcohol withdrawal syndrome that can be life-threatening. Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment for managing alcohol withdrawal symptoms, including delirium tremens. However, in patients with severe liver disease, it is crucial to choose a benzodiazepine that is metabolized more safely in this population.
  • Lorazepam is preferred over other benzodiazepines like diazepam and chlordiazepoxide because it has a shorter half-life and undergoes glucuronidation, a metabolic pathway that is less affected by liver dysfunction. This makes lorazepam safer for patients with impaired liver function.
  • Thiamine (vitamin B1) is important to administer in patients with alcohol use disorder to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, but it is not the treatment of for delirium tremens.

questions.stem: The side effects of lithium in psychiatry practice includes all except?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hypocalcemia


Hypocalcemia (low calcium levels in the blood) is not a side effect of lithium therapy. In rare cases, lithium may cause hyperparathyroidism and elevated parathyroid hormone levels, which can lead to hypercalcemia (elevated calcium levels in the blood).

Other options:

 

Lithium is a mood stabilizer commonly used in the treatment of bipolar disorder. The common side effects of lithium include:

 

Option A. Nausea and vomiting: Gastrointestinal disturbances, such as nausea and vomiting, are common side effects of lithium, particularly during the initial stages of treatment.

 

Option B. Tremors: Fine tremors are a well-known side effect of lithium therapy. These tremors may be dose-dependent and can be reduced by lowering the dose or by adding a beta-blocker.

 

Option D. Hypothyroidism: Lithium can interfere with thyroid function, leading to hypothyroidism in some patients. Regular monitoring of thyroid function is recommended during lithium treatment.

questions.stem: A psychotropic drug inhibiting the reuptake of serotonin is likely to cause which of the following side effects?
questions.solutionHtml:
an dir="ltr" lang="EN-US" style="font-size:12.0pt">Ans. B) Sexual dysfunction

 

Explanation:

 

  • SSRIs are commonly used to treat depression and anxiety disorders. They work by increasing the levels of serotonin in the brain, which helps regulate mood. However, SSRIs can also cause several side effects, including sexual dysfunction. This can manifest as decreased libido, difficulty achieving orgasm, or erectile dysfunction.
  • The other side effects listed (dry mouth, visual disturbance, and constipation) can be associated with other types of psychotropic medications but are not as commonly linked to serotonin reuptake inhibitors.

Explanation:

 

  • Mirtazapine is an atypical antidepressant drug.
  • It inhibits presynaptic α2 receptors and thus increases NA and 5-HT release due to inhibition of auto- and hetero- receptors, respectively.
  • There is selective activation of 5-HT1 receptors due to antagonistic activity at 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors. So, mirtazapine is also known as noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant (NSSA).

  • Sexual dysfunction is not a problem with this drug.

questions.stem: Dysphoria caused by opiates is mediated by which receptor?
questions.solutionHtml:
span style="font-family:Calibri,sans-serif">Ans. B) Kappa

 

Explanation:

 

  • The dysphoria caused by opiates is mediated by the kappa opioid receptor. The kappa receptor is one of the three major classes of opioid receptors (the other two being mu and delta) and is found throughout the central and peripheral nervous systems.
  • When activated, the kappa receptor produces a variety of effects, including analgesia, dysphoria, and sedation. The dysphoric effects of kappa receptor activation are thought to be due to its effects on the reward pathway in the brain, which can lead to feelings of discomfort, anxiety, and aversion.
  • In contrast, activation of the mu opioid receptor is associated with the pleasurable effects of opioids, including pain relief and euphoria. The delta receptor is less well understood but is thought to play a role in the modulation of pain perception and mood.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old teacher began to experience changes in mood. He was losing interest in his work and lacked the desire to play his daily tennis match. He was preoccupied with feelings of guilt, worthlessness, and hopelessness. In addition to the psychiatric symptoms, the patient complained of muscle aches throughout his body. Physical and laboratory tests were unremarkable. After 6 weeks of therapy with fluoxetine, his symptoms resolved. However, the patient complains of sexual dysfunction. Which of the following drugs might be useful in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
ns-serif">Ans. D) Mirtazapine

 

Explanation:

 

  • In this case, the patient has experienced sexual dysfunction as a side effect of fluoxetine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). Switching to another medication with a lower risk of sexual side effects may be helpful. Most typical antidepressants including SSRI, SNRI, MAO inhibitors and TCA can cause sexual adverse effects, so atypical antidepressant drugs are better option in this patient.

Other Options:

Option A,Option B and Option C : Fluvoxamine, Sertraline and Citalopram are SSRI which may also cause sexual side effects whereas Mirtazapine is an atypical antidepressant that acts as an antagonist at alpha-2 adrenergic receptors and serotonin receptors (5-HT2 and 5-HT3). It has a lower risk of causing sexual side effects compared to SSRIs.
